notes.meaning: Paul speaks to Christian slaves, mostly those whose masters were not believers. They were to give their masters real respect, not just outward obedience. If Christian slaves became rude or rebellious, outsiders would blame God and the gospel for it. Commentators add that urging patience under hardship did not mean Paul approved of slavery.

Some slaves had masters who were fellow Christians. Being brothers in Christ did not give them the right to look down on these masters. Being equal before God did not cancel their duties on earth. They should serve even better, because the people helped by their work were believers loved by God. Timothy was to teach this and urge people to live it.

Some people were teaching a different message. Paul measures them against the "sound" or healthy words of Jesus Christ. He also points to teaching that leads to godliness, which means a life that honors God. Christ's words heal the soul and keep a church healthy.

Such a teacher is puffed up with pride, yet he really understands nothing. He has a sick craving for arguments over words. That brings envy, quarrels, insults, suspicion and endless friction. Their minds have gone bad, and they treat religion as a way to make money.

Paul turns the false teachers' idea around. Godliness really is great gain. The gain is not money but good for the soul, now and forever. It comes when godliness goes together with contentment, which means being satisfied with what God gives.
We arrived in the world with nothing, and we will leave with nothing. This echoes Job's words. So there is no reason to grab anxiously for more. Even the richest person takes only a grave in the end.

Food and clothing stand for life's real needs. The word for clothing means "covering," which may include a home. If God gives us what we truly need, we should be content. Paul is not forbidding comfort. He is warning against making wealth our goal.

Paul does not say "those who are rich" but "those who want to be rich," meaning people set on getting wealth at any cost. That desire opens the door to temptation. It is a trap, and it leads to many foolish and harmful wants. The picture is a ship sinking to the bottom, a complete ruin.

The problem is the love of money, not money itself. That love is a root from which all kinds of evil grow. Some people chased after money and wandered away from the faith. They wounded themselves with deep sorrows, such as a guilty conscience.

differ.view: Some read it as "the root of all evils." They say the love of money means wanting what money buys instead of God, so it truly lies behind every evil.

notes.meaning: "Man of God" speaks first to Timothy as a minister. It also fits every Christian who belongs to God. Timothy must run from the love of money and chase better things. These are righteousness (doing right by others), godliness (honoring God), faith, love, endurance and gentleness.

The picture comes from athletic contests. The Christian life is a real struggle against sin and temptation, and it is a good fight. Timothy must grab hold of eternal life the way a winner grabs the prize. He had once made a public confession of faith before many witnesses, and that promise still held him.

differ.view: Baptist teachers see the good confession as the public confession Timothy made at his baptism.
The "many witnesses" point to Timothy's ordination, when he was set apart for ministry.
Methodist teachers have suggested his baptism, or a time when he stood firm while imprisoned for Christ.

notes.meaning: Paul gives Timothy a solemn charge before God, who gives life to all things and can raise his servants even if they die. He also charges him before Christ, who boldly told Pilate the truth about his kingdom. Timothy must keep this command spotless and blameless. Paul means the whole charge and the gospel way of life. He must keep it until Jesus appears again.

God will bring about Christ's return at the right time. That time is not for us to know. God is blessed and perfectly happy. He is the only true Ruler, and every earthly king gets his power from him. The title "King of kings" is also given to Jesus in Revelation.

Only God has immortality in himself. Any other being that lives forever receives that life from him. He lives in light too bright for anyone to come near, and no human eye can see him. We know him only as he shows himself through Christ, and believers will one day see him in some way. Paul ends with praise.

Paul does not tell rich believers to throw their wealth away. He warns them against pride and against trusting money, which can vanish overnight. They should put their hope in God instead. He generously gives us all things to enjoy.

The rich should use their wealth to do good. Their good works should be as plentiful as their riches. They should give freely and be glad to share with others. Wealth is worth most as a chance to do more good.

By giving now, they store up treasure for the future. Jesus spoke of treasure in heaven in the same way. It is a surprising truth: they store up by giving away. So they take hold of the life that is truly life. This is not earned by gifts, but comes through God's free mercy.

Timothy must guard what has been entrusted to him. Paul pictures it as money deposited with a banker. It is the gospel truth, which Timothy received and did not invent. He must turn away from empty, irreverent talk. He must also turn from false "knowledge" that argues against the gospel. Real knowledge would agree with the gospel.

Some people who claimed this so-called knowledge drifted away from the faith. Paul closes with a blessing of grace, God's undeserved kindness. Grace includes all that is good. Where God gives grace, he will also give glory.
